phonemes.desc: A soft bilabial fricative [β] between vowels, made with both lips rather than the teeth; lighter and voiced compared with the English 'f'
Short open-mid back rounded [ɔ], the o-ogonek; it is the u-umlaut of a, written ö in Modern Icelandic, and is never the long vowel
A true final cluster [st]; the r before it is a full alveolar trill and no vowel is inserted between the s and the t

pronunciation.approximation: 'BIV-rost' — stress the first syllable; let the f pass as a soft breath between the lips, almost a 'v'; say the ǫ as a short, open 'aw' cut in half, not the long 'oh' of the English Bifrost.

kin.label: Old Norse manuscript variant
kin.form: Bilrǫst, the reading of the Poetic Edda's Codex Regius (Grímnismál, Fáfnismál), with bil 'moment, interval of time' in place of bifa

kin.label: Modern Icelandic
kin.form: Bifröst, with ö continuing the medieval ǫ

kin.label: Alternate name
kin.form: Ásbrú, 'the Æsir-bridge', the name the gods themselves give it in Grímnismál

pronunciation.note: Cleasby–Vigfusson (s.v. bifrǫst) glosses the name 'the trembling way,' from bifa 'to shake, tremble' and rǫst 'a league, a distance to be traversed'; Zoëga (s.v.) gives the same etymology and records the alternate name Ásbrú 'the Æsir-bridge.' The Eddic codex reads Bilrǫst, with bil 'moment, lapse of time,' and editors still debate which compound is original; Snorri's Bifrǫst is the form that prevailed. The o-ogonek ǫ is a distinctive atomic letter that the ASCII form loses, so the restoration is Tier 1 under the mechanical rule.

domains.title: Rainbow, Fire, Threshold
domains.subtitle: The domain of Bifrǫst
domains.lead:
In the norse tradition, Bifrǫst is the burning rainbow that joins Miðgarðr to Ásgarðr — the trembling path, from bifa 'to shake' and rǫst 'a league, a distance to be traversed.' The gods themselves call it Ásbrú, the Æsir-bridge, and ride it daily to hold court beneath Yggdrasill.

The name encodes a structure built to fail: strong beyond any other work, as Snorri insists, yet fated to shake, to burn, and at last to break beneath the sons of Muspell. Between its watchman's horn and its final shattering, the bridge is the measure of the distance between gods and everything else.

cards.name: The Trembling Way
cards.desc: From bifa 'to shake' and rǫst 'league, path': the bridge is a trembling span of three colors, made with more skill and cunning than any other structure.

cards.name: The Red Band of Fire
cards.desc: Snorri explains the red stripe as burning fire: the bridge is warded in flame so that frost-giants and mountain-giants cannot climb it into heaven.

cards.name: Heimdallr's Watch
cards.desc: At Himinbjǫrg, where the bridge reaches heaven's edge, Heimdallr keeps guard — hearing the grass grow, seeing a hundred leagues by night, holding the Gjallarhorn.

cards.name: The Breaking at Ragnarǫk
cards.desc: When the sons of Muspell ride over it toward the field of Vígríðr, the bridge shatters beneath them; the horses of the gods must swim the flood.

symbols.name: The red band
symbols.meaning: The stripe of burning fire within the rainbow that bars the giants from heaven

symbols.name: Gjallarhorn
symbols.meaning: Heimdallr's horn, kept at the bridge and winded to wake the gods at Ragnarǫk

symbols.name: Himinbjǫrg
symbols.meaning: 'Heaven's castle,' Heimdallr's hall at the bridge's head where it touches the sky

symbols.name: Urðr's well
symbols.meaning: The spring beneath Yggdrasill where the gods ride each day to sit in judgment

symbols.name: The horses of the Æsir
symbols.meaning: The steeds named in Grímnismál — Glad, Gyllir, Glær, Skeiðbrimir and the rest — that bear the gods over the burning span

mythology.lead: Bifrǫst is the one road between the worlds of gods and men, and every story told of it is a story about passage: who may cross, what the crossing costs, and what happens when the road itself gives way. Snorri describes it as the strongest of all constructions and yet builds its destruction into the end of the world. The poems of the Codex Regius, which read the name as Bilrǫst, already know that the bridge will break. Around it gather Heimdallr the watchman, the daily assize at Urðr's well, and the solitary figure of Þórr, who is forbidden the span and wades the rivers instead.

myths.title: The Bridge of Three Colors
myths.text:
Gangleri asks how the gods pass from heaven to earth, and Hárr answers that they built Bifrǫst from earth to heaven: a bridge of three colors, very strong, and made with more skill and cunning than any other work. The red in the rainbow, Hárr explains, is burning fire, so that the frost-giants and mountain-giants cannot mount into heaven over the bridge.

At the bridge's head, where it reaches the edge of heaven, stands Himinbjǫrg, the hall of Heimdallr, the watchman of the gods. He needs less sleep than a bird, sees a hundred leagues by night as by day, and hears the grass growing on the earth and the wool on the sheep. Beside him waits the Gjallarhorn, whose blast is heard in all worlds.

myths.title: The Daily Ride to Judgment
myths.text:
Every day the Æsir ride up over Ásbrú — the Æsir-bridge — on their named horses, to sit in judgment at the ash Yggdrasill. But Þórr does not ride. Grímnismál says that he must wade the rivers Kǫrmt and Ǫrmt and the two Kerlaugar each day on his way to the doomstead, for the Æsir-bridge stands all aflame and the holy waters seethe.

Snorri gives the same exception a physical cause: the thunder-god's passage, with the heat and weight of his thunder, would break the span. The strongest of the gods is thus the one who walks — the bridge that carries everyone else cannot carry him.

myths.title: The Shattering at Vígríðr
myths.text:
When the end comes, Heimdallr stands and winds the Gjallarhorn to wake the gods. Surtr advances from the south with fire, and behind him ride the sons of Muspell toward the field of Vígríðr. They ride over Bifrǫst, and the bridge breaks beneath them.

The poets of the Codex Regius knew it already: Fáfnismál says that Bilrǫst breaks as the hosts ride across, and the horses must swim in the surge, and Grípisspá repeats the prophecy. The road between worlds is the first great work of the gods to fall — the connection is severed before the battle is even joined.

syncretism: The burning rainbow has no attested continental Germanic counterpart — no Old English or Old High German source names the bridge, so Bifrǫst belongs to the Old Norse material alone, and any deeper common-Germanic pedigree is conjecture. Comparanda crowd around it nonetheless. In Greek tradition Iris is the rainbow made person, the messenger who moves between heaven and earth along the arc; in the Rig Veda the rainbow is Indra's bow (Indradhanush), a weapon hung in the sky; and the rainbow covenant of Genesis 9 was familiar to the Christian Icelanders who copied the Eddas, a juxtaposition that colors, though it does not explain, Snorri's red band of fire. In Finnic and Baltic folklore the Milky Way is a road of birds or souls, another shining path overhead. Later European folk belief kept the rainbow as a bridge and a boundary — the treasure at its foot, the impossibility of reaching its end — and modern popular culture, most openly Marvel's Einstein–Rosen 'Bifrost,' has translated the trembling way into a wormhole, which is the same intuition in newer physics: a bridge that burns, shakes, and cannot be trusted to hold.
culturalLegacy: Wagner fixed the bridge in the modern imagination at the close of Das Rheingold: Donner's hammer summons the storm that clears the air, the rainbow appears, Froh names it as the way to the gods' new castle, and the gods process over it into Valhalla while Loge mutters that they are hastening toward their end — a reading of Bifrǫst's built-in doom that Snorri would have recognized. Nineteenth- and twentieth-century book illustration kept the burning arc as the standard emblem of the passage to Ásgarðr. Marvel's comics and films made Bifrost a household word, reimagining it as a wormhole guarded by Heimdall and gate-keeping travel between realms; games from God of War Ragnarök to Assassin's Creed Valhalla render it as the shimmering road between worlds. Modern heathen practice uses the rainbow bridge as a symbol of the live connection between Miðgarðr and the gods, while the unrelated 'Rainbow Bridge' poem of pet bereavement shows how far the idiom of the shining span has travelled from its Old Norse root. Restoring Bifrǫst in Unicode keeps the trembling in the name — the ASCII Bifrost has forgotten that the bridge shakes.
extendedMeditation: Some names are nouns; this one is a verb wearing the shape of a thing. Bifrǫst means the trembling way, and everything the tradition says about it honors that grammar: a bridge of fire and color that the gods trust daily and that is fated, precisely because it connects what must be kept apart, to fail at the last. To name a structure after its shaking is to admit that connection is always provisional — that the distance between heaven and earth is not abolished by the bridge but measured by it. Unicode restoration returns that admission to readable form.

archaeology: Bifrǫst is a textual figure with no known pictorial or runic attestation: no picture stone, amulet, or runestone names or unambiguously depicts the rainbow bridge, and the riders carved on stones such as Ardre VIII cannot be securely tied to it. Its transmission is manuscriptal. The mythological poems that preserve it — Grímnismál, Fáfnismál, Grípisspá, Lokasenna, Vafþrúðnismál — survive in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270), which reads the name as Bilrǫst. Snorri's extended account in Gylfaginning survives in the Codex Regius of the Prose Edda (GKS 2367 4to, early fourteenth century), the Codex Wormianus (AM 242 fol.), the Codex Upsaliensis (DG 11), and the Codex Trajectinus (Traj 1374), whose divergences editors weigh stanza by stanza.
originalScriptNote: The name is Old Norse Bifrǫst, transmitted in Latin-script codices; no runic inscription preserves it. In a normalized Younger Futhark rendering it would be written ᛒᛁᚠᚱᛅᛋᛏ, with ᛅ for the ǫ. The ǫ is the o-ogonek, the u-umlaut of a — a short open-mid vowel, written ö in Modern Icelandic — and it is the one distinctive feature the ASCII form destroys. The restored registrable form is bifrǫst.com (punycode xn--bifrst-zcc.com); the ASCII fallback bifrost.com flattens the trembling vowel into a plain 'o'.
